title: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
summary: How Jepsen tests real databases on real clusters: clients record invoke and completion histories while a nemesis injects partitions, pauses and clock faults, then Knossos and Elle check the claimed consistency.
outcomes: Explain why consistency bugs hide on healthy clusters and how a Jepsen test's control node, clients, nemesis and checker fit together
Record operations as ok, fail or info correctly and explain why a mislabeled timeout creates false alarms
Decide by hand whether a small register history is linearizable and explain why checker cost grows with concurrency
Choose nemesis faults (partition shapes, pauses, clocks) that target a given failure-handling mechanism
Infer ww, wr and rw edges from list-append observations and classify the resulting cycle as G0, G1c, G-single or G2

lessons.title: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs

blocks.md: From the consensus course you know that Raft and Paxos keep replicas agreeing on a log as long as a majority can talk. Databases built on top of them make promises to their users: *linearizable* keys, *serializable* transactions, writes that are never lost once acknowledged. This course is about checking those promises from the outside, the way Jepsen does.

The trouble is that most of the dangerous code paths only run when something goes wrong: a leader is cut off by the network, a process freezes for a few seconds, a clock jumps. On a healthy cluster every replica agrees, so a test suite that never breaks anything will pass even when the failure handling is wrong. Unit tests also tend to test one component with mocks, while the bug lives in how many real processes interact.

**Jepsen** is a Clojure library by Kyle Kingsbury for *opaque-box* testing: it runs the real database binaries on a real cluster, talks to them only through their normal client API, and judges them only by what clients observe. It never peeks at internal state, so whatever it reports is something a real user could have seen.

blocks.title: One Jepsen test: control node, five DB nodes, one history

scenes.caption: Everything on the left runs as one Clojure program on the control node. It logs into the DB nodes n1 to n5 over SSH and installs the real database binaries there.
The generator hands invocations to logically single-threaded processes. Each process owns a client that talks to the database over its normal network API.
The same generator also schedules fault operations for the nemesis, a special process bound to no node. Here it cuts n4 and n5 off from the others while clients keep working.
Every operation's start (invoke) and end (completion) is appended to the history, including the nemesis's own operations, so faults can be lined up against client results later.
After the run the checker reads the whole history and asks one question: is there any way this history could have come from a system that keeps the promised consistency model?

blocks.md:
A few terms you will use throughout:

- **Process**: a logically single-threaded actor that performs one operation at a time through its own client.
- **Generator**: the schedule of operations (reads, writes, faults) and their timing.
- **Nemesis**: the process that injects faults such as partitions, crashes, pauses and clock changes.
- **History**: the list of every invocation and completion, in the order they happened.
- **Checker**: code that decides whether the history is consistent with a model of correct behavior.

Jepsen judges a system only by its history: what clients asked for and what they were told. A violation is reported only when **no** legal execution of the claimed model could explain that history, so a failure is a real bug, not a guess.

Results land on the control node under `store/<test-name>/<date>/`, with the history, logs and the checker's verdict. The method has an honest limit that every Jepsen report repeats: testing can prove the presence of bugs, never their absence. A clean run means this workload with these faults found nothing.

blocks.question: Why does Jepsen insist on talking to the database only through its client API instead of reading each replica's internal state?
options: The promise being tested is about what clients observe, so a violation in the client-visible history is exactly a broken promise
Internal state is too large to copy over SSH quickly
Opaque-box tests run faster because no instrumentation is needed
Most databases encrypt their on-disk state
blocks.explain: Consistency models are defined over the operations clients perform and the results they get back. If the client-visible history is impossible under the claimed model, the system broke its promise, whatever the internals look like. Speed and encryption are not the reason.

blocks.question: A team runs its integration tests 10,000 times on a five-node cluster with no faults and never sees a lost write. What does that tell you about lost writes during a leader change?
options: They cannot happen, because 10,000 runs is statistically enough
They are impossible because Raft guarantees committed entries survive
Very little: leader changes never happened in those runs, so the code that handles them was barely exercised
They can only happen if the disk is corrupted
blocks.explain: Without injected faults the failure-handling paths rarely run at all. Raft's guarantee covers committed log entries; bugs often live around it, in reads served outside the log, client retries, or leases. Repetition of a run that never triggers the path proves nothing about it.

lessons.title: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info

blocks.md: A Jepsen *operation* is a small map. The generator emits an invocation such as `{:type :invoke, :f :write, :value 3}`; `:f` names the function and `:value` its argument. Jepsen does not interpret `:f` or `:value` at all. Only your client and your checker give them meaning.

The client's `invoke!` function applies the operation to the database and returns a *completion* with one of three types:

- `:ok`: the operation definitely happened, with this result.
- `:fail`: the operation definitely did **not** happen.
- `:info`: we do not know. It may have happened, may not, or may still happen later.

If `invoke!` throws an exception, Jepsen converts it into an `:info` completion automatically, which is always the safe default.

blocks.code:
(invoke! [_ test op]
  (try+
    (case (:f op)
      :read  (assoc op :type :ok,
                    :value (parse-long-nil (v/get conn "foo" {:quorum? true})))
      :write (do (v/reset! conn "foo" (:value op))
                 (assoc op :type :ok))
      :cas   (let [[old new] (:value op)]
               (assoc op :type (if (v/cas! conn "foo" old new) :ok :fail))))
    (catch java.net.SocketTimeoutException e
      (assoc op :type (if (= :read (:f op)) :fail :info), :error :timeout))
    (catch [:errorCode 100] e
      (assoc op :type :fail, :error :not-found))))
blocks.caption: The etcd register client from the Jepsen tutorial. A timed-out read becomes fail, a timed-out write or cas becomes info, and etcd's key-not-found error on cas is a definite fail.

blocks.prompt: A write times out after 5 seconds during a partition. A tidy engineer changes the client so every timeout returns `:fail`, to keep the history clean. What happens when a later read returns the value of that write?
blocks.reveal: The checker now believes the write never happened, so a read of its value looks like a value appearing from nowhere. It reports a consistency violation that is **not real**: the database applied the write and simply could not acknowledge it in time. Mislabeling an unknown outcome as `:fail` produces false alarms (and wastes days of debugging). Only report `:fail` when you know the operation had no effect.

blocks.title: A timed-out write stays concurrent with everything after it

scenes.caption: Healthy cluster. Each operation is a bar from its invocation to its completion: write 1 ok, read returns 1, compare-and-set from 1 to 2 ok.
At 3 s the nemesis partitions the network. Process 0 invokes write 3 at 3.5 s and waits. The client's request timeout is 5 s (the value used in the Jepsen tutorial).
At 8.5 s the timeout fires. Did the write happen? Nobody knows, so the completion is info. The checker must treat it as possibly taking effect at any time from now to the end of the test.

Process 0 counts as crashed: it may still have a request in flight, so it never runs again. Jepsen gives the worker thread a fresh process id, and the new process reads 3. The info write really did happen.

blocks.md: Why can a timed-out operation stay "open" forever? The request may sit in a queue, in a replica's log, or in a retry loop, and be applied seconds later. So the checker treats every `:info` operation as **concurrent with everything that happens after its invocation**. And because the original request may still be in flight, the process that issued it is considered crashed and never performs another operation; its thread continues under a new process id.

Reads are the exception the tutorial points out: a read does not change state, so whether a timed-out read happened or not makes no difference to anyone else. Turning crashed reads into `:fail` is safe, and it matters for speed, as the next lesson shows.

Misconception: "a timeout means the request failed." A timeout means *you stopped waiting*. Writes, compare-and-sets and transaction commits that time out must be recorded as `:info` unless the error proves nothing was applied (for example, the request was rejected before it was sent).

blocks.question: Which completion in a client is a bug?
options: A read that timed out is recorded as fail
A write whose commit request was sent but whose socket then closed is recorded as fail
A cas that got etcd's key-not-found error is recorded as fail
A write that threw an unexpected exception is recorded as info
blocks.explain: Once the request has been sent, the database may have applied it, so the outcome is unknown and must be info. The read case is safe because reads have no effect, the key-not-found error proves the cas did not apply, and exceptions becoming info is Jepsen's default.

blocks.question: A test with 5 client processes runs for 10 minutes and 40 writes end as info. Roughly how many operations can be concurrent near the end of the history?
options: At most 5, because there are only 5 processes
Exactly 40, the info writes alone
Zero, because the test is over
Up to about 45: the 5 live processes plus 40 writes that might still take effect
blocks.explain: Each info write stays open until the end of the history, and the crashed processes were replaced by fresh ones that keep issuing operations. So concurrency near the end is the live processes plus every unresolved info op, which is what makes checking expensive.

lessons.title: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order

blocks.md: For a single key, the strongest common promise is **linearizability** (Herlihy and Wing, 1990): every operation appears to take effect atomically at some instant between its invocation and its completion, and the results match a sequential execution in that order. That instant is the operation's *linearization point*. Because the point must lie inside the operation's window, real time constrains the order: if A completes before B is invoked, A must come first.

To check a history, you also need the sequential behavior of the object, called the **model**. Jepsen's Knossos library defines models as pure step functions: given a state and an operation, return the next state, or an *inconsistent* marker if the operation is impossible from that state.

blocks.code:
(defrecord CASRegister [value]
  Model
  (step [r op]
    (condp = (:f op)
      :write (CASRegister. (:value op))
      :cas   (let [[cur new] (:value op)]
               (if (= cur value)
                 (CASRegister. new)
                 (inconsistent (str "can't CAS " value " from " cur " to " new))))
      :read  (if (or (nil? (:value op)) (= value (:value op)))
               r
               (inconsistent (str "can't read " (:value op) " from register " value))))))
blocks.caption: The compare-and-set register model from Knossos, as shown in the Jepsen tutorial. A read of nil always passes, which covers reads that never returned a value.

blocks.md: The checker's job is a search: is there **some** order of operations that respects every real-time constraint and that the model accepts step by step? Let us run it by hand on a tiny history. Every count below comes from a brute-force script that tries all 24 orders.

blocks.prompt: Process 2's read (rA) returns 2 and the later read rB returns 1. Both writes acknowledged ok. Before playing scene 4, decide: is there any legal order?
blocks.reveal: No. After rA reads 2, the register must hold 1 again before rB, so write 1 must take effect after rA. But write 1 completed at 2 ms and rA was invoked at 3 ms, so write 1's point must be before rA's. The brute-force search confirms 0 legal orders out of the 3 that respect real time. Knossos would report something like *can't read 1 from register 2*: a **stale read**.

blocks.title: Finding linearization points in a four-operation history

scenes.caption: A register starting empty. write 1 and write 2 overlap, so either may take effect first. rA overlaps write 2. rB starts after everything else has finished.
Real time forces three orderings: write 1 before rA, rA before rB, write 2 before rB. Of the 4! = 24 orders of these operations, only 3 respect them.
One of the 3 is legal for a register: write 1, rA reads 1, write 2, rB reads 2. Each point sits inside its own bar, so the history is linearizable.
Swap the read results. Now none of the 3 real-time orders works: once rA has seen 2, write 1 would have to land after rA, but write 1 finished before rA began. Not linearizable.

Same reads, but write 1 timed out as info, so its bar runs to the end and process 0 is crashed (rB now runs on process 1). 8 of 24 orders respect real time and write 2, rA, write 1, rB is legal. Uncertainty lets the history pass.

blocks.md: Scene 5 is the price of uncertainty. An info operation's window never closes, so it can be placed almost anywhere, and histories that would fail with a definite `:ok` now pass. The checker stays *sound* (it never reports a fake violation) but becomes less sensitive. That is another reason to return `:fail` whenever you truly know an operation did not happen.

blocks.title: Orders to consider for c concurrent operations (c!)

scenes.caption: With c operations all overlapping, any of the c! orders could be the real one. Up to 5 it is tiny: 6, 24, 120.
Each extra concurrent operation multiplies the count: 720, 5040, 40320 at c = 8. Every info op adds one to c for the rest of the history.

blocks.md: Checking linearizability is NP-complete in general, and Knossos's cost grows explosively with concurrency. Knossos ships a graph search (`knossos.linear`) and a tree search (`knossos.wgl`), plus a `competition` mode that runs both in parallel; the Elle paper notes these build on techniques from Wing and Gong and from Lowe. Pruning and symmetry help, but they cannot change the shape of the problem.

The practical fix is to keep each checked history small. Operations on different keys linearize independently, so Jepsen's `independent` namespace lifts a single-key test to many keys: values become `[key value]` pairs, each key gets a bounded run (the tutorial uses 10 processes per key and 100 operations per key), and the checker analyzes every key's sub-history separately.

Linearizability checking is a search for one legal order inside the real-time constraints. Its cost is driven by how many operations overlap, so you control it by limiting operations per key and by turning known non-effects (like timed-out reads) into `:fail`.

blocks.question: Your Knossos check runs out of memory on a 20-minute register test. Which change helps most without weakening what the test can detect?
options: Split the workload across many independent keys with a bounded number of operations per key
Lower the number of nemesis faults to zero
Record every timeout, including writes, as fail
Remove all reads so only writes are checked
blocks.explain: Independent keys bound concurrency and length per checked history, which is what drives the search cost. Removing faults removes the bugs you were looking for, recording write timeouts as fail creates false alarms, and without reads there is nothing to contradict.

blocks.question: A history contains write 5 (ok, 0 to 1 ms), then read (ok, 2 to 3 ms) returning 5, then write 6 (info, from 4 ms), then read (ok, 9 to 10 ms) returning 5. Is it linearizable?
options: No: write 6 was invoked, so the later read must see 6
Yes: the info write 6 may never have taken effect, or may take effect after 10 ms
No: two reads can never return the same value
It cannot be decided without the server logs
blocks.explain: An info operation may or may not take effect, and if it does, its point can lie anywhere after its invocation, including after the final read. So write 5, read 5, read 5 (with write 6 omitted or last) is a legal order.

lessons.title: The nemesis: partitions, pauses, clocks and crashes

blocks.md: The **nemesis** is a special client, not bound to any node, that injects faults. Like other processes it takes operations from the generator, typically pairs like `{:type :info, :f :start}` and `{:f :stop}`, so faults are scheduled in the same timeline as client operations and are recorded in the same history.

blocks.caption: Adapted from the tutorial (which takes the time limit from the command line): clients issue a random mix of reads, writes and cas about every 1/50 s, while the nemesis waits 5 s, starts a partition, waits 5 s, heals. With a 30 s limit that gives partitions over 5 to 10, 15 to 20 and 25 to 30 s.

blocks.md:
Jepsen's built-in faults, all applied to the real nodes over SSH:

- **Partitions**: a *grudge* maps each node to the nodes it must ignore, and each node gets `iptables -A INPUT -s <peer> -j DROP` rules. Healing flushes the rules.
- **Kill**: kill the database process and restart it later.
- **Pause**: `SIGSTOP` the process, later `SIGCONT`. A paused node is alive but silent, like a long GC pause.
- **Clock**: bump a node's clock by an offset, or strobe it back and forth rapidly.
- **Packet**: delay, drop, corrupt, duplicate, reorder or rate-limit packets with `tc` and netem.
- **File corruption**: truncate files or flip bits in data files.

blocks.title: Who can talk to whom under each partition spec

scenes.caption: Healthy five-node cluster: 1 means the two nodes can exchange packets, 0 means the nemesis drops them.
:one isolates a single random node (here n1). The other four still form a majority of 3 or more and can elect a leader.
:majority shuffles the nodes and bisects them, smaller half first: here n1 and n2 against n3, n4 and n5. Only the side with 3 nodes has a majority.
:majorities-ring (ring order n1 to n5 here; Jepsen shuffles it). Every node sees exactly 3 nodes, a majority, but no two nodes see the same majority. Connectivity is not transitive.

blocks.md: The partition *specs* in Jepsen's combined nemesis choose shapes that stress quorum logic differently. `:one` and `:majority` are clean splits. `:minority-third` cuts off fewer than a third of nodes (1 of 5), useful for Byzantine-tolerant systems. `:majorities-ring` is the nasty one: every node can see a majority, so every node may think it can make progress. `:primaries` isolates nodes that the test believes are leaders.

blocks.prompt: You know Raft never commits two different entries at the same log index. So how could a Raft-based store return a stale value during the `:majority` partition above?
blocks.reveal: By answering reads **outside** the log. A deposed leader in the minority does not know it lost leadership until it hears a higher term. If it serves reads from local state, it returns values that a newer leader has already overwritten. Raft's log safety is intact; the read path skipped it. This is exactly what Jepsen found in etcd in 2014, and why etcd added quorum reads.

blocks.title: A stale read from a deposed leader

scenes.caption: n1 leads and the register holds 3. The nemesis splits n1 and n2 from n3, n4 and n5. n1 has not heard anything yet, so it still believes it is leader. (Simplified to four actors.)
The majority side times out and elects n3 in term 2, exactly as Raft prescribes. Two nodes now believe they lead, in different terms.
Client A writes 4 through n3. n3 replicates it to n4 and n5, a majority, and acknowledges. The write is committed.
Client B reads from n1, which answers from its local state without consulting a majority. B gets 3 after the write of 4 completed: not linearizable.
With a quorum read the request must go through consensus. n1 cannot reach a majority, so the read times out instead of lying. Unavailable, but correct.

blocks.md: Pauses expose a different class of bug: anything that relies on time-based leases. In the etcd 3.4.3 analysis, Jepsen protected updates to a shared set with etcd locks, as the etcd docs suggested. With two-second lease TTLs, five concurrent processes and process pauses every five seconds, it could reliably induce the loss of about 18% of acknowledged updates. A paused lock holder resumes after its lease expired and someone else took the lock, then writes as if it still held it.

A distributed lock alone cannot guarantee mutual exclusion: a holder can be paused or delayed past its lease. The etcd report recommends fencing: pass a monotonically increasing token (such as the lock key's revision) with every protected operation, and have the protected resource reject tokens older than the newest it has seen.

Start broad, then narrow. Jepsen's combined nemesis package is meant for throwing many simple faults (partition, packet, kill, pause, clock, file corruption) at the system to see what sticks. Once something fails, restrict the faults and targets to reproduce it faster.

blocks.question: A coordination service hands out locks that expire if the holder misses heartbeats for 2 s. Which nemesis is most likely to show two clients holding the same lock?
options: Process pauses with SIGSTOP and SIGCONT lasting longer than the lease
A partition that isolates one follower that holds no locks
Bit flips in a log file on a single node
Packet duplication on a client link
blocks.explain: A paused holder cannot notice its lease expiring, so another client acquires the lock, and the first resumes believing it still holds it. Isolating an uninvolved follower or flipping bits does not target the lease mechanism.

blocks.question: In the `:majorities-ring` partition on five nodes, what does each node see?
options: Only itself
Exactly two neighbors plus itself, a majority, and a different majority from every other node
All four other nodes, but with delay
Two nodes in the minority and three in the majority, cleanly split
blocks.explain: Each node keeps links to its two ring neighbors, so it sees 3 of 5 nodes. That is a majority, but the majorities overlap rather than coincide, so connectivity is not transitive, a case that clean splits never exercise.

lessons.title: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions

blocks.md:
Registers are fine for single keys, but databases sell multi-key **transactions** with isolation levels like serializable or snapshot isolation. You could treat the whole database as one object and run a linearizability search, but that explodes even faster, and serializability checking is NP-complete in general with no real-time order to prune the search. The Elle paper reports that Knossos often timed out or ran out of memory after a few hundred transactions.

*Serializable* means the outcome matches some one-at-a-time order of the transactions. *Snapshot isolation* (SI) means each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken when it starts and commits only if no concurrent transaction wrote the same keys.

Elle (Kingsbury and Alvaro, 2020) instead builds Adya's **direct serialization graph**: one vertex per transaction, edges for dependencies on versions of the same object.

- **ww**: Tj installs the version right after one Ti installed (Tj overwrote Ti).
- **wr**: Tj read a version Ti installed.
- **rw** (anti-dependency): Ti read a version and Tj installed the next one (Ti did not see Tj's write).

Anomalies are cycles: **G0** uses only ww edges, **G1c** uses ww and wr edges, **G2** has at least one rw edge, and **G-single** has exactly one. G1a (reading an aborted write) and G1b (reading an intermediate write) are checked directly.

The catch: clients never see the database's version order. With blind register writes, two transactions that set x to 1 and 2 leave no trace of which came first. Elle's trick is to choose a workload whose reads reveal history. Each object is a list, each write appends a value unique across the test, and each read returns the whole list. That gives **traceability** (a read of [1, 2, 3] implies versions [], [1], [1, 2], [1, 2, 3] in order) and **recoverability** (every value maps to the one transaction that appended it).

blocks.code:
; one completed transaction in the history: micro-ops over keys
{:type :ok, :f :txn,
 :value [[:r 34 [2 1]] [:append 36 5] [:append 34 4]]}

; check a whole history against a claimed model
(elle.list-append/check {:consistency-models [:serializable]
                         :directory "out"}
                        history)
blocks.caption: Elle's list-append shape: reads return the full list, appends add a unique element. In SQL databases the list can be a TEXT column updated with CONCAT.

blocks.md:
Here is a real case from the paper's TiDB study (TiDB claimed snapshot isolation). Three transactions, observed by clients:

- T1: read key 34 as [2, 1], append 5 to key 36, append 4 to key 34
- T2: append 5 to key 34
- T3: read key 34 as [2, 1, 5, 4]

blocks.title: Key 34 as an append-only list reveals its own history

scenes.caption: T3 read key 34 as [2, 1, 5, 4]. Because every append adds a unique value at the end, that one read tells us the versions went [], [2], [2, 1], [2, 1, 5], [2, 1, 5, 4] in exactly that order.
Recoverability: each value was appended by exactly one transaction, so 5 maps to T2 and 4 maps to T1.
T1 read key 34 as [2, 1]. The next version after [2, 1] was installed by T2's append of 5, so T1 did not see T2: T1 rw T2 (anti-dependency).
T1 also appended 4, directly after T2's 5. So T2's version came first: T2 ww T1. T1 must be both before and after T2.

blocks.title: The inferred dependency graph and its cycle

scenes.caption: T1 read [2, 1] and missed T2's append of 5, so T1 must be ordered before T2. That is an rw (anti-dependency) edge from T1 to T2.
T3 read the version T1 installed, [2, 1, 5, 4], so T3 comes after T1: a wr edge. Harmless on its own.
T1's append of 4 directly follows T2's 5, so T2 is also before T1: a ww edge from T2 to T1. Together with the rw edge that is a cycle.
The cycle T1 to T2 to T1 has exactly one rw edge: G-single (read skew). No serial order can explain it, and snapshot isolation forbids it too, so a database claiming SI is caught.

blocks.md: Every step was a linear-time inference: index who appended what, take the longest read of each key as its version order, derive edges, then find cycles with Tarjan's strongly connected components in O(V + E). The paper reports Elle checking histories of hundreds of thousands of transactions in tens of seconds, where Knossos stalled at a few hundred. Elle can also add process (session) and real-time edges to separate strict serializability from plain serializability.

The TiDB anomalies came from an automatic retry mechanism, enabled by default, that re-applied a conflicting transaction's writes without re-checking; disabling it revealed a second, undocumented retry mechanism. In the same paper Elle found G2-item cycles in YugaByte DB when masters crashed or paused, and transactions in FaunaDB that failed to observe their own prior writes.

Elle never solves for a transaction order. It designs the workload so reads expose the version order, then turns the history into a dependency graph and looks for cycles. A cycle is a concrete, explainable counterexample, and its edge types name the anomaly.

Elle is sound but not complete. A cycle found is real, yet missing cycles prove nothing: appends never observed by a later read leave gaps in the version order, and predicate anomalies (like phantoms over WHERE clauses) are outside its analysis.

blocks.question: Why does Elle prefer append-only lists over read-write registers?
options: Lists are cheaper to store than integers
A read of a list reveals the whole sequence of prior versions, so the version order (and ww and rw edges) can be inferred from client observations alone
Registers cannot be read inside transactions
Lists make every transaction commit, so there are no aborts to analyze
blocks.explain: A blind register write destroys history: you cannot tell which of two writes came first. A list read like [1, 2, 3] traces every version in order, and unique values recover who wrote each one.

blocks.question: Elle reports a cycle T1 wr T2, T2 rw T3, T3 rw T1. How is it classified?
options: G0, because it is a cycle
G1c, because it contains a wr edge
G2, because it has two rw edges
G-single, because it has exactly one rw edge
blocks.explain: The cycle has two anti-dependency (rw) edges, so it is G2 but not G-single. G1c cycles contain only ww and wr edges; G0 only ww. Two rw edges is the shape of write skew, which snapshot isolation allows but serializability forbids.

blocks.question: A snapshot-isolated database is tested with Elle and the report shows only G2 cycles with two or more rw edges, no G-single, no G1. What should you conclude?
options: The database violates snapshot isolation
The history is consistent with snapshot isolation, though not with serializability
Elle failed, because a real system always shows G0
Nothing, because Elle cannot classify cycles
blocks.explain: Snapshot isolation forbids G0, G1 and G-single and allows G2 cycles whose rw edges are adjacent, like write skew. If two rw edges were never adjacent (Elle calls this G-nonadjacent), SI would be violated. Only a claim of serializability makes adjacent-rw G2 a violation, and a clean run never proves SI holds in general.
